question: The three main divisions of the ear, from the outside inward, are:

options.text: Outer ear, middle ear, inner ear
Pinna, iris, lens
Eustachian tube, optic nerve, semicircular canal
Cochlea, cornea, retina

explanation: Sound (and balance information) passes from the outer ear, through the air-filled middle ear, to the fluid-filled inner ear, which houses both the hearing organ (cochlea) and the balance organ (vestibular apparatus).

question: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the back of the throat, and its main function is to:

options.text: Equalize air pressure on both sides of the eardrum as ambient pressure changes
Produce the fluid found in the inner ear
Carry sound vibrations directly to the brain
Detect angular acceleration during turns, since the tube sits close to the semicircular canals and relays information about the rate of turning to the brain

explanation: Without a way to equalize pressure, a changing ambient pressure (such as during a climb or descent) would leave the eardrum bowed and painful. The Eustachian tube, opened by swallowing or yawning, vents the middle ear to match outside pressure.

question: Repeated, prolonged exposure to loud engine or cabin noise without hearing protection most typically leads to:

options.text: A gradual, often permanent, loss of hearing sensitivity, particularly at higher frequencies
Improved ability to detect very quiet sounds over time
No measurable long-term effect, since the ear fully recovers after each flight
A temporary loss of balance with no effect on hearing, since the noise produces only a brief disturbance to the vestibular system which settles within a few minutes of landing

explanation: Noise-induced hearing loss accumulates with repeated exposure and is frequently irreversible once the sensory hair cells in the cochlea are damaged, which is why hearing protection (headsets, earplugs) is routinely recommended around aircraft.

question: The vestibular apparatus, located in the inner ear, is primarily responsible for sensing:

options.text: Light intensity for pupil control
Motion and orientation of the head — rotational movement and linear acceleration including gravity
Blood oxygen saturation, which is measured by the inner ear through the pressure of the fluid and reported to the brain as a continuous signal during the entire flight
Sound frequency and volume

explanation: The vestibular system is the body's own motion sensor, built from structures that respond to turning (the semicircular canals) and to linear acceleration and gravity (the otolith organs) — it has nothing to do with hearing itself, despite sharing the same inner-ear space.

question: The semicircular canals of the inner ear specifically detect:

options.text: Linear acceleration only, such as speeding up in a straight line
Angular acceleration — changes in the rate of turning about an axis
Air pressure changes in the middle ear
Colour and brightness of light, since the semicircular canals contain light-sensitive cells that react to changes in illumination as the aircraft moves through the sky

explanation: The three semicircular canals, oriented roughly at right angles to each other, are filled with fluid that lags behind during a change in rotational speed, bending sensory hairs and signalling angular acceleration about that axis — not steady-state rotation, and not linear motion.

question: A pilot enters a sustained, constant-rate turn. After the fluid in the semicircular canals catches up with the aircraft's rotation, the pilot's vestibular system will:

options.text: Stop signalling any turning at all, even though the aircraft is still turning at a constant rate
Continue to signal the turn accurately for as long as it lasts
Signal a turn in the opposite direction, since the fluid in the canals keeps moving against the direction of rotation and so produces a sensation of reverse turning
Signal increasing turn rate the longer the turn continues

explanation: The semicircular canals only respond to a change in rotation rate, not to a steady rotation itself. Once the fluid inside stops lagging and moves with the canal, no further signal is produced — which is exactly why a sustained, constant-rate turn can feel, after a short while, like no turn at all.

question: After the scenario above, if the pilot now rolls the wings level to stop the turn, the semicircular canal fluid will:

options.text: Produce a sensation of climbing rather than turning
Instantly stop moving with no further sensation, since the fluid in the canals settles at once when rotation ends and the pilot receives no sensation of any kind afterwards
Signal the correct, now wings-level, attitude immediately
Briefly continue moving, now signalling a turn in the opposite direction even though the aircraft is flying straight

explanation: Stopping the turn is itself an angular deceleration, which the canal fluid registers as a turn in the opposite direction. This false sensation of turning — the somatogyral illusion, also called "the leans" — can tempt a disoriented pilot to roll back into the original turn to "correct" a turn that no longer exists.

question: During a rapid acceleration in level flight, such as a go-around with a sudden increase in thrust, a pilot may experience:

options.text: No vestibular sensation at all, since acceleration only affects hearing
A false sensation of descending, since the otolith organs respond to any change in airspeed by signalling a nose-down attitude, which the pilot must correct immediately in flight
A sensation of turning that has nothing to do with acceleration
A somatogravic illusion — a false sensation of pitching nose-up, because the otolith organs cannot distinguish forward linear acceleration from a true change in pitch

explanation: The otolith organs sense the combined effect of gravity and linear acceleration, and the brain cannot tell the two apart from vestibular input alone. Strong forward acceleration tilts that combined vector backward, which the brain misreads as the body — and the aircraft — pitching up, even when the actual pitch attitude has not changed.

question: A somatogravic illusion during a go-around is particularly hazardous because a pilot who believes the aircraft has pitched up too far may be tempted to:

options.text: Ignore the flight instruments entirely, which is the correct response
Extend the landing gear, which resolves the illusion, since the change in drag and the sound of the gear locking in place give the pilot a clear and immediate sense of the true attitude
Increase thrust further, which has no bearing on the illusion
Push the nose down in response to the illusion, losing altitude at exactly the point a climb is required

explanation: Trusting the false sensation rather than the attitude indicator can lead a pilot to push the nose down during exactly the phase of flight — a low-altitude go-around — where height is most needed. This is why instrument reference, not bodily sensation, is the standard guard against somatogravic illusions.

question: The standard defence taught against both somatogyral and somatogravic illusions is to:

options.text: Trust the flight instruments over bodily sensation whenever the two disagree, especially with no reliable outside visual reference
Make control inputs based on how the aircraft "feels"
Reduce airspeed to zero to stop all vestibular input
Close the eyes and rely entirely on the inner ear, since the vestibular system is the most reliable source of attitude information once the outside view has been lost

explanation: The vestibular system is easily fooled by exactly the conditions flight often creates — sustained turns, strong accelerations, no visible horizon. Instrument flying exists precisely because it gives an objective reference that bodily sensation, in these illusions, cannot be trusted to provide.

question: Alcohol affects the vestibular system in a way that can produce a specific, well-documented illusion because it:

options.text: Improves the accuracy of the balance system temporarily
Improves the accuracy of the balance system temporarily, since a small amount of alcohol stabilises the fluid in the canals and sharpens the pilot's response to every movement
Diffuses into the fluid of the semicircular canals at a different rate than into the surrounding canal tissue, unbalancing the system's normal response to motion
Permanently destroys the vestibular apparatus after a single drink

explanation: Because alcohol moves into the canal fluid and the surrounding tissue at different rates as blood alcohol rises and later falls, the density balance the canals rely on is disturbed, producing false sensations of rotation (positional alcohol nystagmus) that can persist well after drinking has stopped.

question: Motion sickness is generally explained by a "sensory conflict" theory, meaning it arises when:

options.text: Symptoms occur only when the eyes are closed, because with no visual input the inner ear alone cannot signal body position, and the brain then has nothing to resolve the conflict
The motion signalled by the vestibular system does not match the motion (or lack of it) suggested by vision and other senses
A person has eaten too soon before flying, regardless of any motion
Only the eyes are involved, with no contribution from the inner ear

explanation: The classic example is reading in the back seat of a moving car, or below deck on a boat: the eyes report a stationary scene (the page or cabin) while the vestibular system reports real motion. The mismatch between these signals, more than the motion itself, is what the sensory conflict theory holds responsible for the resulting nausea.

question: A passenger prone to motion sickness in turbulence is generally best advised to:

options.text: Read a book to distract themselves from the motion
Look toward a stable outside visual reference, such as the horizon, rather than reading or looking at a fixed point inside the cabin
Move to the row with the least fresh air, because stale air is the main cause of motion sickness and it is quickly relieved by a change of seat during the flight
Keep their eyes closed for the entire flight

explanation: Looking at the horizon gives the eyes a visual motion cue that roughly matches what the vestibular system is sensing, reducing the sensory conflict. Reading, by contrast, gives the eyes a stationary scene while the body is genuinely moving — the exact mismatch that provokes symptoms.

question: Information from the eyes, ears and other sense organs is first carried to the brain through:

options.text: The bloodstream, carried as hormones
Direct muscular reflexes that bypass the central nervous system entirely, so that the brain receives the information only after the body has already responded to it
Sensory nerves that form part of the peripheral nervous system
A single nerve shared by all senses

explanation: Each sense organ has its own dedicated sensory nerve pathway carrying signals from the periphery to the central nervous system, where the brain integrates them into a coherent picture of the outside world.

question: Vision and hearing together provide the large majority of the information a pilot uses to fly, which is significant because:

options.text: Touch alone is sufficient to fly an aircraft safely
Any factor that degrades either of these two senses has an outsized effect on overall situational awareness compared with a similar effect on a minor sense
Smell is the dominant sense used for navigation, because olfactory cues from fuel and hydraulic fluid tell the pilot exactly where the aircraft is on the approach path
All senses contribute exactly equally, so no single sense matters more than another

explanation: Because vision and hearing carry so much of the information load in flying, conditions that degrade them — glare, noise, fatigue, hypoxia — have a disproportionately large effect on a pilot's overall awareness compared with an equivalent effect on a less-used sense.

question: The otolith organs, part of the vestibular apparatus, respond primarily to:

options.text: Linear acceleration and the constant pull of gravity
Changes in blood pressure in the cerebral arteries, which the otolith organs detect and use to judge the aircraft's attitude and speed when flying in cloud
Air pressure changes in the middle ear
Rotational acceleration only

explanation: Unlike the semicircular canals, which sense turning, the otolith organs contain tiny crystals that shift under linear acceleration and gravity, giving the sense of "up" and of speeding up or slowing down in a straight line.

question: A disoriented pilot who has unknowingly entered a gentle, sustained turn in cloud is at particular risk because:

options.text: The attitude indicator becomes unreliable during any turn, because its gyroscope is disturbed by the same rotation that the vestibular system senses in the inner ear
Gentle turns cannot be sustained for more than a few seconds
The attitude indicator becomes unreliable during any turn
The vestibular system may have already stopped signalling the turn, so the pilot feels wings-level even though the attitude indicator shows otherwise

explanation: Because the semicircular canals only detect changes in turn rate, a smoothly entered, constant-rate turn can quickly feel like straight flight to the pilot, even as the instruments correctly show a bank. Trusting that false wings-level feeling over the instruments is exactly how a graveyard spiral can develop.

question: A hearing protection device (such as a well-fitted headset) is most useful on the flight deck because it:

options.text: Reduces cumulative noise exposure while still allowing radio communication and alerts to be heard clearly
Eliminates the need for sterile cockpit procedures, since a headset that blocks all cabin and cockpit sound removes the need for crews to keep distractions to a minimum
Has no effect on long-term hearing but improves comfort only
Completely blocks all sound, including radio calls

explanation: Good headsets attenuate the broadband engine and airflow noise that causes cumulative hearing damage while still passing speech and warning tones clearly, which is why they protect hearing without compromising communication.

question: Pain felt in the ear during a rapid descent, when the Eustachian tube fails to equalize pressure quickly enough, is a form of:

options.text: Motion sickness, because the inner ear is stressed by the rapid pressure change during the descent and the resulting disturbance spreads to the balance organs nearby
Barotrauma — tissue stress caused directly by a pressure difference across the eardrum
Decompression sickness
Hyperventilation

explanation: If the Eustachian tube cannot vent the middle ear fast enough to match the changing cabin pressure, a pressure difference builds across the eardrum, straining it directly — a mechanical injury (barotrauma), not a gas-bubble or motion-related condition.

question: The "graveyard spiral" is a well-known hazard in which a disoriented pilot:

options.text: Experiences the illusion only in clear daylight conditions, because bright visual cues make the pilot more likely to notice a steepening spiral and correct the bank in time
Misjudges a developing bank and turn as wings-level, and in correcting an apparent descent by pulling back, tightens the turn and steepens the spiral
Is unaffected by any vestibular illusion during the event
Experiences the illusion only in clear daylight conditions

explanation: In a graveyard spiral, a sustained turn has faded from the pilot's vestibular sense, so an unnoticed bank develops along with a descent. Pulling back to arrest the perceived sink, without first levelling the wings, actually tightens the turn and steepens the descent — the classic trap this illusion sets.
